prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B014 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The achievement is a specific invention: a lattice at the magic wavelength cancels the differential light shift, so a very large number of atoms can be interrogated on a narrow clock transition without perturbing it. That is a different principle from the comb that reads out the clock and from the single-ion control behind the 2012 prize, where the stability comes from one ion rather than from averaging over many atoms. The consequence is demonstrated, not promised: clock-to-clock comparisons near 1e-18 in several laboratories and species, centimetre-level relativistic geodesy, and tighter limits on constant variation and ultralight dark matter. The credit maps onto the history with two names, Katori for the concept and first realization, Ye for taking it to the accuracy frontier and for the many-body clock work. I have not changed my preferred configuration. What I have changed is the citation, which I now word around magic-wavelength lattice trapping and the accuracy it allowed, because Pearce, Olsson and Mehlig are right that wording drifting toward optical frequency metrology in general would reopen 2005 and 2012. I also considered whether the chair's last question calls for a two-part prize. With B014 using two of the three permitted names, a second part could carry only one person, and none of the alternatives has a one-name core that I could defend, so I do not propose one.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously after reading the files is the one from Danielsson, Johansson and Mehlig: that the lattice clock may be a refinement of a recognised precision-measurement programme, with the discovery content smaller than a new classification of phases. I think the magic-wavelength idea answers that, but I concede it is a judgment about kind of achievement rather than a fact I can prove. Second, the SI second has not yet been redefined; I regard this as a supporting application and not a criterion, as Pearce says, but a committee could still prefer to wait. Third, the credit is clean only if one accepts that Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemke, the ion-clock groups and the PTB, Paris and NIST teams have no claim that outweighs that of the two named. Priority details are from recollection and I have not verified them against nomination text. Finally, B016 is a strong competitor: if the committee judges that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be set aside, it is a mature and conceptually broad prize, and I would not call a vote for it unreasonable.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B016 first as a closed theory-to-experiment chain with greater conceptual originality, and accepts B014 as the better-attributed alternative while asking whether the lattice clock is a new discovery or a refinement of precision measurement.
responses.response: To your discriminating question I would say that the magic-wavelength condition is an original physical idea, not an engineering refinement: before it, trapping atoms in a lattice meant accepting light shifts that destroyed the transition frequency, and the idea that a particular wavelength makes the shift vanish is what opened the many-atom regime. On criteria, I would put attribution first, since you grant that B014 is cleaner, and then ask whether the discovery is distinct from prior prizes. On your own account B016 needs the uncredited HgTe proposal to be set aside and carries a 2016 overlap risk, while B014 carries a 2005 and 2012 risk that I think a precise citation controls. If the committee concluded that a citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice cannot be separated from the comb, that would move me toward B016, so I name that as my reason for moving, and I do not treat the larger opening support as a reason.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B016 because it changes how band structure and symmetry are understood and has a full prediction-to-observation chain, and she ranks B014 as a transformative instrument for an already well-defined measurement; she also says the pending SI redefinition makes B014 easy to defer.
responses.response: I take the distinction between a conceptual framework and an instrument seriously, but I do not think the prize categories separate them that way: the physics prize has honoured both and the instrument cases were rewarded when they opened a new regime of measurement. Here the regime is real, since uncertainty near 1e-18 turns a clock into a sensor of gravitational potential at the centimetre level and of possible constant variation. I agree with you that the pending redefinition is no ground for delay or for urgency. You also note that HgTe edge quantization is imperfect and Zhang is deceased, which leaves B016 with an experimental half that is less clean than its theory half. That difference in attribution and in experimental cleanness is the main reason I stay with B014, and I have not been moved by the observation that your conceptual argument is stronger in kind, though I accept it is the strongest point against my position.

responses.point: Johansson keeps B016 first for its closed prediction-and-confirmation loop but says B014 is her honest second choice and the cleaner two-person allocation if the HgTe attribution cannot be defended, while arguing that a lattice-clock prize rewards metrological performance more than a new physical effect.
responses.response: I agree with you that if the committee cannot defend omitting the HgTe proposers, B014 is the cleaner allocation, and that is the conditional structure I would like the committee to test explicitly. I disagree that the lattice clock rewards performance more than a physical effect. The cancellation of the light shift at a magic wavelength is a statement about atomic structure and polarizability, and the many-body and collisional shifts in dense lattices that Ye's group controlled are physics in their own right. I accept your point that the redefinition of the second is a timing argument, and I do not rely on it. I also take your remark on imperfect HgTe quantization as a real weakness of the experimental half of B016, though not a disqualifying one.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved to B014 on attribution and confirmation and wants the citation written around magic-wavelength trapping and the accuracy it allowed, and asks whether the committee is relying on counts.
responses.response: I accept your wording constraint and have adopted it in my citation. I also share your concern about counts: the opening and round-1 tallies of four, three and one are not a scientific argument, and I have tried to rest B014 on attribution, reproduction and distinctness from 2005 and 2012. On the chair's question about a two-part prize, I considered it and find that the three-name ceiling makes it impractical, since B014 already uses two names and I cannot defend a one-name second part from the shortlist. I would not change that unless a member shows a one-name core that stands alone.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B018 for the influence of DMFT on how correlated-electron physics is done, but accepts that B014 is the least risky candidate on attribution and that B016 and B014 are more decisively theory-meets-experiment.
responses.response: I accept that DMFT is mature and influential and I agree that nobody has argued otherwise. Our difference is on the kind of achievement. The point you make against your own candidate, that Metzner cannot be fitted under the three-name ceiling and that it is a method whose quantitative predictivity depends on double-counting and parameters, is the reason I would not lead with it. I would resist reading B014 as the third step in a line of precision-spectroscopy awards, because those earlier prizes recognised the comb and single-ion control, and the lattice clock stands on a different principle, but I agree the risk is real and the citation must manage it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize; I think a precisely worded citation does this, but the answer is a committee judgment.

Whether the claims of Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemke and the ion-clock groups, or of the PTB, Paris and NIST teams, outweigh the clean Katori and Ye split; priority details are recalled from general knowledge and not verified against the nominations.
Whether the committee should wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second, which I do not regard as a criterion.
Whether the chair rules that my Boulder connection requires recusal from B014 or only disclosure, and whether my judgment is influenced by familiarity with this community.
How the committee should weigh B016's conceptual reach against B014's clean attribution if it is satisfied on neither of the two other criteria.
statement.conflict_note: Update of my round-1 disclosure in answer to the chair's question. As a doctoral student I spent a research period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye's group works in the same Boulder research environment. My profile records no collaboration, joint publication or supervisory tie to Katori or Ye, and the stay was decades ago, so my view is that disclosure is sufficient and recusal is not required for B014. The decision belongs to the chair and the committee, not to me: if it is judged that disclosure is insufficient, I accept being recused from advocating and voting on B014, and members should then read my position as stated here without counting it. I also disclose that my own field, quantum optics and quantum memories in rare-earth crystals at Lund, with WACQT and European quantum-memory collaborations, is close to B005, B008 and B022, though none of these touches the preferred configuration. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp.
